CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue the trade talks constructively to lock in the pause on the List 3 tariff hike and secure a deal that rolls back existing Section 301 tariffs, while using the Huawei/Meng leverage without letting it derail the tariff track. Avoid new escalation — we cannot afford a return to the 25% List 3 hike or fresh tariff rounds on top of an already-falling export base — but do not pre-commit to sweeping structural/tech-transfer reform before concrete tariff relief is on the table. Hold our negotiating line and press for reciprocal concessions.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high but not existential. US Section 301 tariffs now cover ~$250B of Chinese goods (List 1 $34B + List 2 $16B at 25%, List 3 $200B at 10%) and are demonstrably biting: exports plunged 20.7% y/y in February, imports fell 5.2%, and Jan–Feb exports to the US dropped ~14% (Reuters/Globe/Fox, Mar 8). That maps to the CHN '+0.5' anchor (major export sectors hit, firm-level targeting). Huawei adds a second front: the US unsealed charges and Canada voted on Mar 1 to proceed with Meng's extradition, which Beijing frames as 'political persecution' of a high-tech enterprise (NPR Mar 1/6; Politico Mar 3) — a direct threat to our tech-champion ambitions. Offsetting this are the two suspended List 3 hikes (Feb 24 and the Mar 1 deadline passing without an increase) plus credible progress signals — Wang Yi citing 'substantive progress' and Trump saying talks are 'very, very close' — so I read this as +0.4 rather than +0.5: the escalation is paused and a negotiated off-ramp is live. On action, de-escalation-by-negotiation is right: escalating would make a bad export situation worse and invite the very 25% hike we have paused, while the Huawei case already gives us leverage to keep the conversation going. A mild positive action_score (+0.1, negotiate) reflects continuing talks toward purchases and relief without premature structural concessions while enforcement and IP/tech-transfer issues remain unresolved.
